title: The Staircase

setup.context: I don't usually talk about this part. But you asked what changed my sense of time, and this is most of the answer.

paragraphs.text: I was fifty-five when I fell on the stairs at home. Nothing dramatic at first. I stood up, felt a sharp pain at the back of my head, and sat down again on the step. Jyoti found me there twenty minutes later.
The doctors kept me in hospital for nine days. There was bleeding they had to watch, and for two nights nobody could tell me how much I would recover. I remember the ceiling tiles very well.

Jyoti sat by the bed with a notebook, reading me the cricket scores and then pretending she had not. I asked her once why she bothered. She said someone should be paying attention to something boring while I was too frightened to.
Recovery was slow. I had to learn to walk the stairs again, one step at a time, holding the rail the way a child does. It was humiliating, and it was the most honest I have ever been about my body.
After that I stopped treating the body as a tool to be pushed. It is the thing I walk on, eat with, and laugh through. I have been trying to be kinder to it since.

reflection.insight: The fall that frightens you is rarely the one that teaches you. The ordinary, slow recovery does the teaching.
reflection.question: When did your body last remind you that it is not a machine?

follow_up_options: How long did the recovery take?
Did it change how you teach?

responses_to_follow_ups.long: Most of a year before I could manage the stairs without thinking. Longer before I stopped counting them.
responses_to_follow_ups.jyoti: She said I was a terrible patient, which was true, and that she would take me home only if I promised to rest. I did not promise. I rested anyway, which was her way of winning.
responses_to_follow_ups.teach: Yes. I talk about rest now without apologising for it. It used to sound like weakness to me. It does not anymore.
